summary: Kiribati is an island nation in the central Pacific made up of 33 atolls and islands, straddling the equator and the International Date Line, and deeply threatened by sea-level rise.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In 1888 priests of the French Missionaries of the Sacred Heart arrived in the northern Gilbert Islands and evangelized through schools, catechism and respect for local customs, quickly attracting large numbers of believers. Catholicism is the majority in the northern and central islands, is today Kiribati's largest religion, and the church also runs many secondary schools.

ranking.name: Kiribati Uniting Church
ranking.description: The Kiribati Uniting Church grew out of the Protestant churches established in the 19th century by the American Congregationalists and the London Missionary Society; it is most influential in the southern islands and was closely tied to the British administration during the colonial period. When the church was renamed the Kiribati Uniting Church in 2014, part of the congregation objected and formed a new church of their own.

ranking.name: Kiribati Protestant Church
ranking.description: The Kiribati Protestant Church is a group that split off around 2014 over disagreement with the original church's renaming and direction; it kept the name and traditions of the "Protestant Church", and its followers come mainly from the southern islands with a Congregationalist background.

ranking.name: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints
ranking.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (Mormons) arrived in the 1970s by setting up schools locally, offering English-language education and opportunities to study abroad, and so grew quickly among young people; it is one of the fastest-growing churches in Kiribati.

ranking.name: Baha'i Faith
ranking.description: The Baha'i Faith was brought to the Gilbert Islands by missionaries in the 1950s, and afterward Local Spiritual Assemblies were established on some atolls. It has spread to some extent among Pacific island nations, and Kiribati is one of the countries with a relatively high share of Baha'is.

religion.background: Kiribati's indigenous people traditionally worshiped ancestors and spirits (anti). In 1857 the American Congregationalist missionary Hiram Bingham II came to Abaiang Atoll, and in the latter half of the 19th century Protestant missionaries of the Hawaiian and London Missionary Societies preached in the southern Gilbert Islands; in 1888 Catholic priests of the French Missionaries of the Sacred Heart arrived in the northern islands, forming a pattern of "Catholic north, Protestant south". From 1892 Britain ruled the Gilbert Islands, with the churches controlling schools and health care. After independence in 1979, the Christian denominations and the village meeting house (maneaba) system together form the center of social life.

language.official: English and Gilbertese (Kiribati) are the official languages.

ranking.name: Gilbertese (Kiribati language)
ranking.description: The I-Kiribati are a fairly homogeneous Micronesian people who have used the Gilbertese language on the atolls for thousands of years; in the 19th century missionaries devised a script for it and translated the Bible, and churches and schools thus promoted literacy. Since almost all the island nation's population are I-Kiribati, daily life, broadcasting and parliamentary debate are all conducted in Gilbertese.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English comes from British colonial rule of 1892–1979 and is one of the official languages, used in law, government documents and education from secondary school up. But few people have English as their main language, and the English ability of residents of the rural outer islands is also limited, with use mainly in the capital, Tarawa.

language.history: Gilbertese (also called Kiribati, Te taetae ni Kiribati) belongs to the Oceanic branch of the Austronesian family and is close to other Micronesian languages such as Marshallese and Nauruan. In the mid-19th century the American missionary Bingham II devised a writing system for it in the Latin alphabet and translated the Bible, giving Gilbertese a written form. During British colonial rule English became the language of government and of secondary and higher education. After independence in 1979 Gilbertese and English became official languages together, but daily life is conducted almost entirely in Gilbertese.

ranking.name: Babai (giant swamp taro)
ranking.description: Giant swamp taro (babai) is cultivated for several years in dug pits, and after harvest is roasted, boiled or mashed, often mixed with coconut syrup.
ranking.history: Atoll soil is poor and sandy, and the early I-Kiribati developed a way of cultivating babai by digging pits in the ground, bringing in fresh water and composting with leaves; a single plant often takes several years or even more than ten to harvest. Owning a babai pit represents family wealth and land rights, so it is the most honored food at weddings, festivals and meeting-house feasts. In recent years rising sea levels have caused salt water to seep into the pits, and traditional cultivation is under threat.

ranking.name: Breadfruit
ranking.description: Roasted or boiled breadfruit has a texture like potato, and can also be sliced and fried or made into desserts. It is rich in starch and is an important staple for residents of the outer islands.
ranking.history: Breadfruit is a traditional staple of Pacific islanders, spread throughout Oceania thousands of years ago with the seafaring migrations of the Austronesian peoples. In Kiribati breadfruit trees can grow only where the soil is better, so they are very precious, and in the harvest season the fruit is often exchanged with relatives or shared at meeting-house feasts. It is rich in starch and can be fermented for preservation, an important local food supplementing imported rice and flour.

ranking.name: Pandanus fruit
ranking.description: The fruit of the pandanus (screw pine) can be chewed raw to extract the juice, or cooked into a paste or dried into a long-keeping preserved fruit (kabubu).
ranking.history: The pandanus tree tolerates salt and drought and is one of the few plants that can grow in the poor sandy soil of atolls; the I-Kiribati have developed dozens of varieties. In the past, on sea voyages and deep-sea fishing, people carried dried pandanus as rations, which can keep for years. Its leaves can also be woven into mats and roofing, making it an indispensable plant of atoll life, with traditional knowledge passed down within families through the generations.

ranking.name: Coconut crab
ranking.description: A giant land hermit crab whose shell can grow very large, with sweet meat that is usually boiled or grilled. The crab meat and the fat in the abdomen have a coconut aroma and are regarded as a delicacy.
ranking.history: The coconut crab lives on tropical Pacific and Indian Ocean islands and can crack open coconuts with its strong claws, hence the name. In Kiribati, catching coconut crabs is a traditional skill, often done at night, and the crab is regarded as a delicacy for festivals or entertaining guests. Because of population growth and overharvesting, coconut crabs have become scarce on many inhabited islands.

ranking.name: Coconut raw fish (ika mata)
ranking.description: Fresh raw fish cut into pieces is "cooked" in lemon or lime juice, then mixed with coconut milk, onion and chili. It tastes refreshing with the sweetness of coconut milk, and is often eaten as an appetizer or with rice.
ranking.history: The practice of marinating raw fish in coconut milk and citrus juice is widespread across Pacific islands, and on atolls fishing is the main source of protein, with fresh catches such as tuna easy to obtain. Kiribati's waters hold one of the world's important tuna fisheries, and the government's main income comes from the fishing-rights fees of foreign fishing vessels. The dish is both everyday food and a common sight at weddings, church events and meeting-house feasts.
